title: Chapter 4 — That The Americans Combat The Effects Of Individualism By Free Institutions
paragraphs: Despotism is very timid by nature, and it is never more sure of lasting than when it can keep men apart. All its influence is commonly exerted for that purpose. No vice of the human heart suits it so well as egotism. A despot readily forgives his subjects for not loving him, provided they do not love one another. He does not ask them to help him govern the state. It is enough that they do not aspire to govern it themselves. He brands as turbulent and unruly those who would combine their efforts to promote the prosperity of the community, and, twisting the natural meaning of words, he praises as good citizens those who have no sympathy for anyone but themselves. Thus the vices that despotism produces are precisely those that equality fosters. These two things complete and assist each other, with pernicious results. Equality places men side by side with no common tie between them. Despotism raises barriers to keep them apart. Equality predisposes them not to think of their fellow creatures, and despotism makes general indifference a kind of public virtue.

Despotism, then, which is dangerous at all times, is especially to be feared in democratic ages. It is easy to see that in those same ages men most need freedom. When the members of a community are forced to attend to public affairs, they are necessarily drawn out of the circle of their own interests and pulled, at times, away from self-observation. As soon as a man begins to discuss public affairs in public, he begins to perceive that he is not as independent of his fellow men as he had at first imagined, and that to obtain their support he must often lend them his cooperation.

When the public is supreme, there is no man who does not feel the value of public goodwill or who does not try to win it by gaining the esteem and affection of those among whom he is to live. Many of the passions that chill human hearts and keep them apart are then obliged to withdraw and hide below the surface. Pride must be disguised, disdain dares not break out, and egotism is afraid of itself. Under a free government, most public offices are elective. The men whose lofty minds or ambitious hopes are too narrowly confined in private life therefore feel constantly that they cannot do without the people around them. At such times men learn to think of their fellow men out of ambition, and they often find it, in a way, in their interest to forget themselves.

I may be met here with an objection drawn from electioneering intrigues, the meanness of candidates, and the slanders of their opponents. These are occasions for hostility, and they come more often the more frequent elections become. Such evils are certainly great, but they are temporary, whereas the benefits that go with them remain. The desire to be elected may lead some men to violent hostility for a time. But this same desire leads all men, in the long run, to support one another. And if an election happens to separate two friends, the electoral system brings together permanently a multitude of citizens who would otherwise have remained unknown to each other. Freedom produces private hostilities, but despotism gives birth to general indifference.

The Americans have fought, by means of free institutions, the tendency of equality to keep men apart, and they have overcome it. The legislators of America did not suppose that a general representation of the whole nation would be enough to ward off a disorder at once so natural to the structure of democratic society and so fatal to it. They also thought it would be wise to bring political life into every part of the territory. In this way they would multiply without limit the opportunities for all members of the community to act together, and make them feel constantly their dependence on one another. The plan was a wise one. The general affairs of a country engage only the attention of leading politicians, who gather from time to time in the same places, and since they often lose sight of one another afterward, no lasting ties are formed between them. But if the local affairs of a district are to be conducted by the men who live there, the same persons are always in contact. They are, in a way, forced to become acquainted and to adapt themselves to one another.

It is difficult to draw a man out of his own circle and interest him in the destiny of the state, because he does not clearly understand what influence the destiny of the state can have on his own lot. But if it is proposed to run a road across the end of his estate, he will see at a glance that there is a connection between this small public affair and his greatest private affairs. And he will discover, without anyone showing it to him, the close tie that unites private interest to general interest. So, to interest citizens in the public welfare and to convince them that they constantly need one another in providing for it, far more can be done by entrusting them with the administration of minor affairs than by giving them control of important ones. A brilliant achievement may win you the favor of a people at one stroke. But to earn the love and respect of the people around you, you will need a long succession of small services and obscure good deeds, a constant habit of kindness, and an established reputation for disinterestedness. Local freedom, then, leads a great number of citizens to value the affection of their neighbors and kindred. It perpetually brings men together and forces them to help one another, in spite of the tendencies that divide them.

In the United States the wealthier citizens take great care not to stand aloof from the people. On the contrary, they constantly keep on easy terms with the lower classes: they listen to them and speak to them every day. They know that the rich in democracies always need the poor, and that in democratic ages you attach a poor man to you more by your manner than by the benefits you give him. The size of such benefits brings out the difference of conditions, and this causes a secret irritation in those who profit from them. But the charm of simple manners is almost irresistible. Their friendliness wins men over, and even their lack of polish is not always displeasing. This truth does not take root at once in the minds of the rich. They generally resist it as long as the democratic revolution lasts, and they do not acknowledge it immediately after the revolution is over. They are very ready to do good to the people, but they still choose to keep them at arm’s length. They think that is enough, but they are mistaken. They might spend fortunes this way without warming the hearts of the people around them. These people do not ask them to sacrifice their money, but their pride.

It would seem that every imagination in the United States is strained to invent ways of increasing the wealth and satisfying the wants of the public. The best-informed inhabitants of each district constantly use their knowledge to discover new truths that may increase the general prosperity. If they have made any such discoveries, they eagerly hand them over to the mass of the people.

When we closely examine the vices and weaknesses that those who govern in America frequently display, the prosperity of the people causes surprise, but wrongly so. Elected magistrates do not make American democracy flourish. It flourishes because the magistrates are elective.

It would be unjust to suppose that the patriotism and zeal every American shows for the welfare of his fellow citizens are wholly insincere. Private interest directs the greater part of human actions in the United States as it does elsewhere, but it does not regulate them all. I must say that I have often seen Americans make great and real sacrifices to the public welfare, and I have noted a hundred instances in which they hardly ever failed to give each other faithful support. The free institutions that the inhabitants of the United States possess, and the political rights they use so much, remind every citizen in a thousand ways that he lives in society. At every moment they impress on his mind the idea that it is the duty of men, as well as their interest, to make themselves useful to their fellow creatures. And since he sees no particular ground for hostility toward them, being never either their master or their slave, his heart readily leans toward kindness. Men attend to the interests of the public first out of necessity and afterward by choice. What was deliberate becomes instinct, and by working for the good of one’s fellow citizens one finally acquires the habit and the taste for serving them.

Many people in France consider equality of conditions as one evil and political freedom as a second. When they are forced to yield to the former, they try at least to escape the latter. But I maintain that to combat the evils that equality may produce, there is only one effective remedy, namely political freedom.
